t.segment quebrada verde pachacamac@-12.3,:
Lima is one of the driest capitals on earth, and yet just south of it, in the hills above the Lurín valley, the desert turns green for a few months every year. The Lomas de Quebrada Verde are fog oases, where the winter mist called garúa, rolling in from the cold Pacific between roughly June and October, condenses on the hillsides and brings to life a brief explosion of grass, flowers, cacti and shrubs, attracting birds, butterflies and the people of Lima, who come here to walk. The segment between Quebrada Verde and Pachacamac is part of the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road system, which linked the coast with the highlands.

Pachacamac, at the end of the segment near the mouth of the Lurín river, was one of the most important religious centres of ancient Peru, a sanctuary dedicated to the creator god Pachacamac, whose oracle drew pilgrims from all over the Andes for more than a thousand years before the Incas arrived. The Incas incorporated it into their empire and built a temple to the sun on a hill overlooking the sea. The site, with its adobe pyramids, temples and plazas, has an excellent modern museum.

Riding here means getting out of Lima, which can be a challenge, with heavy, chaotic traffic, aggressive drivers and few rules respected. Once out of the city, the Panamericana Sur runs along the coast, a fast highway through the desert, and the roads up the Lurín valley offer a pleasant escape, with orchards, fields and villages, leading toward Cieneguilla and the highlands. Roads to the lomas are unpaved and dusty. In winter, the coast is grey and humid; in summer, from December to March, it is sunny and hot.

Lurín and Pachacamac have fuel, shops and restaurants, and Lima has everything you could need. The Lurín valley is known for its country restaurants serving traditional dishes like pachamanca, chicharrón and fresh fish from the coast, and on weekends families flock here for lunch. The beaches to the south, such as San Bartolo and Punta Hermosa, are popular with surfers. Bring a windproof jacket for the lomas, as the fog can be chilly.
t.segment casila alto chillaco@-12.1,-76.5:
In the mountains east of Lima, high above the desert coast, a stone path clings to the slopes of the province of Huarochirí. It is a section of the Qhapaq Ñan, the great Inca road system, which in this region linked the sacred coastal sanctuary of Pachacamac with Jauja and the central highlands. The segment between Casila Alto and Chillaco is one of the stretches listed by UNESCO in 2014 as part of the transnational Andean Road System. The Inca engineers built it with retaining walls, steps and drainage channels to cope with the steep terrain and seasonal rains, and parts are still used by local farmers and their animals.

The landscape changes dramatically with altitude. Down in the valleys, the climate is dry and sunny, with cacti and irrigated fields of fruit and vegetables. As you climb, the slopes become greener, with terraces built by pre-Inca and Inca farmers, small villages and grazing land. Higher still, the puna begins, with its cold winds, grass and llamas. The region is known for its traditional festivals and for the Huarochirí Manuscript, a collection of Andean myths written down in Quechua around 1600, one of the most important sources on the ancient religion of the area.

The riding is challenging and spectacular. The roads leading up from the Rímac and Lurín valleys are narrow, winding and often unpaved, with steep drops and hairpin bends. The Carretera Central, the main highway into the mountains, is notorious for heavy truck traffic, and the climb from the coast is relentless, gaining altitude quickly. In the rainy season, from December to March, landslides known as huaicos can block roads and cause serious damage. Altitude sickness is a real risk, so take it easy, drink water and allow your body to adjust.

Chosica, about twenty-five kilometres away, is the nearest large town, with fuel, food and accommodation. It is known for its sunny climate, which makes it a popular escape from the coastal fog of Lima in winter. Ricardo Palma and other smaller towns have basic services. Try pachamanca, meat and potatoes cooked in an earth oven, or fresh trout from the mountain rivers.
t.segment molle huarangal@-12.1,-76.7:
The names tell a story about the land. Molle is the Peruvian pepper tree, with its weeping branches and pink berries, and a huarangal is a grove of huarango, the tough, deep-rooted desert tree that once covered much of the Peruvian coast. Between these two places, in the lower hills east of Lima toward the Lurín valley, runs a short stretch of the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road network. Here the road descended from the highlands toward the sanctuary of Pachacamac on the coast, one of the most important religious centres of the ancient Andes, where an oracle drew pilgrims from far and wide. The segment is part of the UNESCO listing of the Andean Road System.

This is the transition zone between desert and mountain. In the coastal winter, from June to September, a blanket of grey fog known as garúa covers Lima, while just a few hundred metres higher the sun breaks through. On some hills, the fog feeds seasonal oases of vegetation called lomas, which suddenly bloom with flowers and attract birds. The rest of the year, the landscape is dry and dusty, with bare brown hills and green ribbons of irrigated farmland along the rivers.

The riding is a mix of urban sprawl and open country. The roads leading out of Lima are busy and chaotic, with buses, combis and trucks, but as you head up the Lurín valley toward Cieneguilla and beyond, things calm down. The roads wind along the river, past orchards, small farms and weekend restaurants, and then climb into the hills on narrower, steeper routes. Watch out for loose gravel, potholes and the occasional landslide, especially after rain in the highlands.

Chosica, about sixteen kilometres away, is the nearest large town, with fuel and services, and the valley towns along the way have smaller stations and shops. Cieneguilla is popular with Limeños on weekends for its country restaurants, many serving pachamanca, meat and potatoes cooked in an earth oven, and chicharrón, fried pork. Finish with a chicha morada, a sweet drink made from purple corn, and do not miss the ruins of Pachacamac down by the sea if you have time.
t.segment san juan de tantaranche huarochi:
The mountains above Lima rise quickly from the desert coast, and within a couple of hours the city's sprawl gives way to steep valleys, terraced slopes and high villages perched on spurs. The segment of the Inca road between San Juan de Tantaranche and Huarochirí runs through this country, part of the Qhapaq Ñan route that linked the sanctuary of Pachacamac on the coast with the highland centre of Xauxa, crossing near the sacred mountain of Pariacaca.

Huarochirí is famous among historians for a document compiled around 1600, the Huarochirí Manuscript, which records in Quechua the myths and rituals of the people of this region, including stories about Pariacaca and the other mountain gods. It is one of the most important sources for understanding Andean religion before the Spanish conquest. Walking a stretch of the old road, with its stone steps and walls, through a landscape of terraces still farmed today, gives that history a physical presence.

The riding requires commitment. The main route from Lima into the highlands is the Carretera Central through the Rímac valley via Matucana, one of the busiest truck roads in Peru, climbing to the pass at Ticlio at over 4,800 metres. To reach Huarochirí and Tantaranche, you leave the main roads and follow smaller valleys, such as those of the Lurín or Mala rivers, on roads that are often unpaved, narrow and winding, with steep drops and landslides in the rainy season.

The altitude changes are extreme: from sea level to over 3,000 metres in a few hours. Take time to acclimatise, drink water and watch for headaches or dizziness. The weather is dry on the coast but can be cold and wet in the mountains, especially from December to March. The dry season from May to October is best for riding.

Matucana, thirty-seven kilometres away, has fuel, food and basic services, and Chosica, closer to Lima, offers more. In the villages fuel may be scarce, so carry a spare. Food is hearty mountain fare: soups, potatoes, cheese, trout and roasted meats. The people are welcoming, but life is hard in these high communities, and visitors who show interest in their traditions are usually well received.
t.zone b@5.3,-75.7:
North of Pereira, where Risaralda meets Caldas, the coffee country climbs into higher, wilder ground above the deep canyon of the Cauca river. Quinchía, two kilometres from this point, is a hill town in Zone B of the Coffee Cultural Landscape of Colombia, the World Heritage Site inscribed in 2011. Here the coffee farms share the slopes with sugar cane for panela, plantain and forest, and the towns feel less visited than the classic stops further south.

The area has a long history before coffee. Indigenous communities, including the Emberá Chamí, have lived in these mountains for centuries, and gold mining, both ancient and modern, has shaped the landscape and the economy. Quinchía itself sits on a ridge with views over the surrounding mountains, and its central square is a lively meeting place.

Riosucio, ten kilometres away in Caldas, is famous for its Carnival of the Devil, held every two years in January, a riotous celebration with music, poetry, masks and a giant devil figure that mixes Indigenous, African and Spanish traditions. Anserma, another nearby town, has a fine colonial church and a lively market.

Riding here is serious mountain riding. The roads are narrow, steep and winding, often with poor surfaces, potholes and landslides, especially in the rainy seasons. Traffic includes buses, trucks, motorcycles and jeeps loaded with coffee. The views are spectacular, with the Cauca canyon below and the peaks of the Western Cordillera on the horizon. Fog can roll in quickly, and rain can turn roads into mud.

Fuel is available in Quinchía, Anserma and Riosucio. The region's food is simple and filling: sancocho, a hearty soup with chicken or beef, plantains and yucca, and arepas. Coffee is grown and roasted locally, and a cup in a small café on the square, watching the town go by, is the best way to experience the rhythm of life in the mountains. Security has improved greatly in recent years, but it is still wise to ask locally about road conditions and safety before setting out on remote routes.
t.segment sisicaya santa rosa de chontay@-:
The Peruvian coast is a desert, and the road up from Lima to the mountains is one of the most dramatic climbs in the Andes. Sisicaya and Santa Rosa de Chontay lie in the Huarochirí province, in the hills above the Rímac valley east of Lima, where the Inca road once climbed from the coastal plain to the high sierra. This stretch of the Qhapaq Ñan, part of the six-country UNESCO listing of 2014, follows ridges and dry valleys, with stone steps, retaining walls and terraces that are still visible if you know where to look.

Huarochirí has a special place in Andean literature. In about 1600, a Spanish priest in the area had local people tell the old stories of their gods, in Quechua, and the result, the Huarochirí Manuscript, is one of the very few records of Andean religion in the words of the people who lived it. It tells of Pariacaca, the mountain god who fought floods and rivals, and of the spirits that lived in rocks and springs. Reading a few pages before the ride makes the barren hillsides feel inhabited.

The road is the Carretera Central, the highway from Lima to La Oroya, and it climbs from the coastal haze through Chosica, a town of about eighty-eight thousand, past Ricardo Palma, a smaller place of under five thousand, and up the Rímac valley into the sierra. Fuel and food are easy in Chosica and the larger towns, but not on the climb, so fill the tank. The road is paved and winding, but heavy with trucks and buses, and corners are blind, with landslides in the wet season, from December to March. Above Chosica the air thins, the scenery turns to brown rock and cactus, and at the top the road crosses the Ticlio pass, above four thousand eight hundred metres, among the highest paved roads in the world.

The dry season, from May to October, is the best time, with blue skies in the highlands, though the coast sits under a grey blanket of cloud. Altitude sickness is real, so ascend slowly, carry water and a warm jacket, and chew coca leaves or drink coca tea if locals offer it. The valley's orchards, famous for fruit like cherimoya and custard apple, make a sweet stop on the way.
t.historic centre of lima@-12.0,-77.0:
Francisco Pizarro founded Lima in January 1535, laying it out around a plaza that is still called the Plaza Mayor, and for the next three centuries it was the capital of Spain's South American empire. The grid of streets around the plaza is the centre today, a mix of baroque churches, carved wooden balconies in the Moorish style, colonial mansions and government buildings. The cathedral, which holds Pizarro's tomb, stands on one side, and the Convent of San Francisco, with its library and underground catacombs, lies a few streets away.

Lima sits on a desert coast, between the Pacific and the foothills of the Andes, and it is one of the world's driest large cities. What it has instead of rain is a grey, damp mist called garua that settles over the city for much of the year, which is why many locals escape to the sun in summer. The Rimac river, a thin ribbon in a stony bed, runs through the northern edge of the centre. The food, on the other hand, is superb. Lima is regarded as one of the great food capitals of the Americas, with ceviche, anticuchos and pisco sours, and even a modest lunch in the old town is worth the trip.

The riding is another matter. The city has millions of inhabitants, and its roads are loud, fast and crowded, with aggressive buses, improvised lane changes and a casual attitude to rules. The Panamericana runs along the coast, and the Carretera Central heads up into the Andes, climbing quickly to altitude and leaving the traffic behind. You can be in cold air and bare mountains within a couple of hours. It is best to leave the bike in a secure car park in the old centre and walk, since street parking is risky.

Fuel is available everywhere, and Lima has every service a rider could want. The weather is mild, rarely very hot or cold, and the best season for sun is from December to March. Keep your valuables out of sight, stay alert in the quieter streets, and enjoy the plazas in the evening, when the lights come on and the cathedral looks its best.
t.fortifications on the caribbean side of:
Columbus named it Puerto Bello, the beautiful harbour, in 1502, and for once a sailor's first impression was right. Portobelo sits on a deep, sheltered bay on Panama's Caribbean coast, backed by steep green hills, and for two centuries it was the point where the wealth of Peru left the New World. Gold and silver came by sea up the Pacific coast to Panama City, crossed the isthmus on mule trails like the Camino de Cruces, and were loaded here onto the Spanish treasure fleets. Every year, a great fair was held, with merchants and soldiers crowding the little port, and prices and diseases both soared.

The riches attracted pirates. Francis Drake died of dysentery on his ship off Portobelo in January 1596, and the town was attacked and sacked by Henry Morgan in 1668 and captured by the British admiral Edward Vernon in 1739. The Spanish responded by building heavy stone forts of coral limestone around the bay, and their gun batteries and thick walls still face the sea, overgrown with tropical plants and patrolled by iguanas. Together with the fortifications of San Lorenzo, at the mouth of the Chagres river, they are inscribed on the World Heritage list as the Fortifications on the Caribbean Side of Panama.

The road here is a pleasure. From the Panama Canal at Colon, the coastal highway winds along the shore through villages and jungle, with the sea appearing and disappearing between palms, and the surface is mostly good but potholed in places. Heavy tropical rain can cut visibility and cover the road with water, so ride carefully in the wet season, from May to December. The dry months, from January to April, are much more comfortable. Trucks and buses are the main hazard, and the last stretch to the town is narrow and curvy.

Portobelo is tiny, about fourteen hundred people, so bring cash and fill your tank in Colon or on the way before you arrive. Inside the church of San Felipe stands the Black Christ, a wooden statue said to have arrived mysteriously by sea, and every October, thousands of pilgrims in purple robes come for the festival of the Nazareno. Try fried fish with patacones, crisp slices of green plantain, at a stall by the water.
t.samarra south zone@34.1,43.9:
Samarra was, for about fifty years in the ninth century, the capital of the Abbasid caliphate, the empire that stretched from North Africa to Central Asia. Caliph al-Mutasim moved his court here from Baghdad in 836, partly to get his Turkish soldiers away from a restless city, and for half a century a vast new capital spread along the east bank of the Tigris. It was one of the largest cities of the medieval world, a sprawl of palaces, mosques, barracks, racecourses and pleasure gardens, and then it was abandoned, leaving ruins in the desert that are remarkably well preserved because nobody built over them.

The southern zone of the site includes the remains of palaces and gardens, among them the Qasr al-Ashiq, a square palace with courtyards and ornate stucco. Further north stands the great spiral minaret of the Malwiya, built of baked brick to a height of about fifty metres, which is the most famous image of Samarra. The brick, the stucco and the geometry give an idea of the splendour of the Abbasid court, and the site has been a World Heritage site since 2007.

I have to be honest about the riding. This is a part of Iraq where the security situation has been difficult for years, and Samarra suffered attacks in the past, including the bombing of the Askariya shrine in 2006. Anyone considering a visit needs current travel advice, local contacts and a lot of caution, and the idea of a casual motorcycle trip here is not realistic. The land itself is flat desert, brown and hot, with the Tigris cutting a green line through it.

Samarra town is large, with about a hundred and fifty thousand people, so fuel and food exist, but conditions can change quickly. If you do get to see the site, go in the cooler months between November and March, and take water, because summer temperatures are above forty-five degrees. Baghdad lies about a hundred and twenty kilometres south.
The coordinates for this segment fall in the high Andes east of Lima, and I should be plain that I do not know this particular stretch of path in detail, only the landscape and the system it belongs to. It is part of the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road network, a web of about thirty thousand kilometres of paved and stepped paths that linked the empire from Colombia to Chile and Argentina, and which UNESCO listed in 2014 across six countries. A segment named for a portachuelo, a small pass, and a lake, Laguna Escalera, suggests a path that climbs from a valley through a notch in the ridge and drops to a lake on the far side, as Inca roads often do.

Inca engineers built their roads to last. They cut steps into slopes, laid stone paving, built drainage channels and retaining walls, and strung rope suspension bridges across gorges. Runners called chasquis carried messages along the route in relays, and storehouses and rest stations stood at intervals. In these highlands the path might cross puna grassland at four thousand metres or more, with vicuña and alpaca grazing, glacial lakes in the hollows and snow peaks above.

On a motorbike, altitude is the main factor. The Carretera Central, which climbs from Lima toward La Oroya and passes through Ticlio at about 4,800 metres, is a spectacular but demanding road, with lorries, mist and cold. Engines lose power in the thin air, and riders can feel headaches and breathlessness, so go up gradually and drink water. Weather turns quickly, with hail and sleet even in the dry season from May to September, which is the best time. Landslides and roadworks occur in the rainy season, from December to March.

There are petrol stations in the towns along the main road, but not on the side tracks, so fill up in Lima or the last big town and carry a spare. Ask locals about the condition of tracks before committing, and respect any community land. Carry warm layers, a first-aid kit and plenty of water, and tell someone where you are going.
t.samarra centre zone@34.2,43.9:
For a few decades in the ninth century, Samarra was the capital of the Abbasid caliphate, the greatest empire in the world, and it was built in a hurry and abandoned just as fast. The caliph al-Mu'tasim moved his court here from Baghdad in 836, partly because his Turkish soldiers were quarrelling with the townspeople, and the city spread for some forty kilometres along the east bank of the Tigris. It was not until 892 that the capital moved back to Baghdad, and the abandoned palaces and mosques were left to the desert. That is why Samarra is so remarkable for archaeologists: a whole early Islamic city that was never built over.

The Centre Zone in this label covers the part of the city that is still lived in, the modern town of Samarra on the river with a population over a hundred and fifty thousand. Here the main landmark is the Al-Askari shrine, a Shia holy place with a golden dome, holding the tombs of the tenth and eleventh Imams, and it is also the place where the twelfth Imam is believed to have disappeared. The shrine was bombed in 2006, an attack that triggered a wave of violence across Iraq, and it has since been rebuilt. Visiting it as a foreigner needs careful checking of the security situation and local permissions, and I would not assume it is open or safe on any given day.

The countryside is flat, dry and brown, a plain of gravel and irrigated fields along the river, with date palms near the water. Roads from Baghdad run north on the main highway, wide and fast, with checkpoints at intervals, and the surface can be broken by heavy trucks. Summer temperatures are extreme, often above forty-five degrees, and spring and autumn are the only sensible seasons. Dust storms can reduce visibility without warning. Travel here is not casual, and anyone planning a ride should seek current advice from reliable sources.

In the town itself you will find fuel, simple restaurants and tea houses, with grilled river fish on offer in the better places. The Tigris is broad and brown, and the old barrage upstream controls water for the plain. On a clear evening the sky turns orange over the dome, and the call to prayer carries across the roofs.
t.samarra archaeological city@34.3,43.8:
If the Centre Zone of Samarra is the living town, this is the ghost city, a spread of ruins stretching for some forty kilometres along the Tigris, on both banks of the Tigris, listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site. When the Abbasid caliphs built Samarra, they did so on a monumental scale, with palaces, mosques, barracks, racecourses and gardens, all of mud brick and stucco, and as there was no fortified wall, the city simply grew along the river. Today it is a landscape of low mounds, outlines of buildings and a few huge standing structures, which give a sense of the empire's wealth.

The most famous monument is the Great Mosque, built in 848 to 852 under al-Mutawakkil, which for centuries was the largest mosque in the world, with walls of fired brick enclosing a space about the size of several football pitches. Beside it stands the Malwiya, the spiral minaret, a conical tower of brick about fifty-two metres high, with a ramp winding round the outside to the top. Nothing like it survives anywhere else, and it is often compared with the ziggurats of ancient Mesopotamia, which the builders would have known. Insurgents blew the top of it in 2005, and repairs have followed.

Other sites include the Balkuwara palace and the Qasr al-Ashiq, a small circular palace on the river, and a huge palace complex, the Jawsaq al-Khaqani, with its great arched gateway, the Bab al-Amma, overlooking the Tigris. The decoration found here, with carved stucco in what scholars call the Samarra style, was copied across the Islamic world, and Samarra pottery and glass are on display in museums everywhere. Look for the abstract, curving designs of the stucco, which spread to Egypt and beyond.

Visiting is complicated. The site lies about seventeen kilometres from Samarra town, the area has seen conflict, and UNESCO listed it as endangered in 2007. Security checkpoints and permissions are real obstacles, and anyone planning a visit should seek current advice and probably a local guide. The landscape is exposed and flat, with no shade and fierce summer heat, so the best months are March to April and October to November. Fuel and basic supplies come from the town, and you should carry water and sun protection and treat any visit as something to arrange with care.
t.lima@-12.0,-77.0:
Lima sits on the edge of one of the driest deserts on earth, and yet it is a city of more than seven million people, held together by a grey sky that locals call la garúa, a damp, low cloud that hangs over the coast for much of the year and rarely produces rain. The city's coastline rises in cliffs above the Pacific, where the districts of Miraflores and Barranco look out to the surf, and parks, cafes and paragliders occupy the clifftops.

Francisco Pizarro founded the city in 1535 as the capital of Spanish Peru, and for centuries it was the main seat of Spanish power in South America. The colonial centre, with its balconied houses, the cathedral and the Plaza de Armas, has survived earthquakes, and contrasts with the modern business districts. Food is a big reason to come: ceviche, made from raw fish cured in lime juice, is a national passion, and Lima's restaurants are among the best in Latin America.

The southbound Panamericana is where this ride begins, and it is more demanding than it looks. Leaving the city means a long run of dense traffic, buses, minibuses, trucks and mototaxis, with lane discipline that is more suggestion than rule. Beyond the suburbs the road runs through bare desert, with the ocean on one side and sand dunes on the other, pushed by strong afternoon winds. Drive defensively, particularly at night, when slow-moving vehicles can be unlit. Oncoming trucks pass on the shoulder, and speed bumps appear without warning near villages. Stay alert and keep your documents handy for police checks.

South of the city, within an easy day trip, is Pachacámac, a vast pre-Inca sanctuary with temples and pyramids made of adobe, a major pilgrimage centre long before the Incas took over. Further along the coast are Paracas, with its sea lions and desert peninsula, and Ica, a desert oasis town. Lima has fuel stations all over, workshops and every kind of accommodation. Start early, because the exit from the city is slow, and carry water. Layers help, since the coast stays cool and damp in winter.
t.archaeological site of panama viejo@9.0,:
A pirate raid ended one city and started another here. Panamá Viejo, the ruins on the shore east of the modern centre, was founded in 1519 by Pedrarias Dávila as the first Spanish settlement on the Pacific coast of the Americas, and for over 150 years it was the staging post where Peruvian silver was loaded for the crossing to the Atlantic. In 1671 the privateer Henry Morgan crossed the isthmus with a force of buccaneers, took the town and left it burning. The Spanish never rebuilt it on the same site.

What survives is a scatter of stone walls, arches and the tower of the cathedral, which stands on a low rise near the water and can be climbed for a view over the ruins, the bay and the skyscrapers to the west. The site is on the UNESCO list together with the later historic district, and the contrast between the two is the point of any visit: old stones on the edge of a modern boulevard, with the city's towers behind them. Plan an hour or two and go early, because in the Panamanian heat the ruins offer almost no shade.

Getting here by motorcycle means working through Panama City's traffic, which is busy and sometimes aggressive. The Cinta Costera, a waterfront road along the bay, gives a clear and fast run with views of the skyline, but the surrounding streets are heavy with buses, taxis and delivery vans. Rain arrives suddenly in the wet season from May to December, often in the afternoon, and the painted lines turn slippery. The dry months, from January to April, are the best for riding and for the ruins.

Fuel is everywhere in this city of more than a million in its urban area, including right near the site in Parque Lefevre. Cafés and snack stands cluster at the entrance, and fresh coconut water and cold drinks are welcome after the walk. Keep valuables out of sight when parked, and use official parking where possible.

Early on a dry-season morning, when the tide is out and the light is still soft on the stones, is the moment to come.
t.historic district of panama@9.0,-79.5:
After Morgan destroyed the old town in 1671, the Spanish chose a new site a few kilometres west, on a rocky peninsula that was easier to defend, and moved the city in 1673. That is the historic district of Panamá, today called Casco Viejo or Casco Antiguo, and it is a very different place from the ruins. Narrow streets laid out in a grid run past colonial churches, balconied houses and small plazas, with the Pacific on three sides and the glass towers of the modern city across the bay.

Walk around and you can read the layers. The golden altar of San José, the arches of Las Bóvedas along the sea wall, the grand lines of the Teatro Nacional, the pale presidential palace known as the Palace of the Herons for the birds that live in its courtyard: all of them come from different centuries, and the French influence of the canal years in the late nineteenth century shows in the iron balconies and the Plaza de Francia, which honours the failed French canal effort. Some buildings are beautifully restored, some are ruins, and many are somewhere in between. Rooftop bars and restaurants have multiplied, and the streets in the evening are lively.

Riding here is more a matter of parking than of corners. The streets are narrow, mostly one-way, often cobbled or brick, and slippery when wet, and the peninsula can jam at weekends and during events. Go slowly, watch for pedestrians and taxi doors, and leave the bike somewhere secure rather than on the kerb. Panama City's wet season, from May to December, brings sudden downpours; the dry months from January to April bring the best weather.

Fuel is not available on the peninsula itself, but plenty of stations lie a few minutes away in the main part of town. Coffee here is excellent, since Panama grows some of the world's most expensive beans, and a cup in a café on a shaded plaza is a good reason to linger.

The best time is early evening, when the heat drops and the sea wall fills with people.
East of Lima, the land climbs fast. The Rímac valley begins at the coast as a green ribbon through the desert and rises toward the Andes, and Santa Rosa de Chontay and Molle lie in the foothills above Chosica, a town of nearly ninety thousand about ten kilometres off. Here the coastal fog that blankets Lima for much of the year gives way to sun, which is why Chosica earned the nickname of the city of the sun and why wealthy Lima families kept weekend houses here.

This segment belongs to the Qhapaq Ñan, the great Inca road network, which ran along both coast and mountains for thousands of kilometres. Roads like this one climbed from the Pacific valleys toward the high passes, linking the oracle at Pachacamac on the coast with the highland centres, with stone steps, retaining walls and way stations built for runners and llama trains. Little of the stonework looks dramatic, but a path cut into a steep slope and still walkable five hundred years later is more impressive than it sounds.

For the rider, the modern road beside the old one is the Carretera Central, the Central Highway, which climbs up the Rímac valley past Chosica and Matucana to the pass at Ticlio, about 4,800 metres, one of the highest paved passes in the world. The road has fine curves, tunnels and drop-offs, and heavy truck traffic that grinds up the grades in clouds of diesel. In the rainy months, from January to March, landslides called huaycos can bury sections of road, so check conditions before you set out. The railway that follows the valley reaches a summit station higher than any other standard-gauge line.

Fuel is easy in Chosica, which has stations on the main street, but it thins out above Matucana, so top up before climbing.
