Nearby reserves protect the gallito de roca, the Andean cock-of-the-rock, a flame-orange bird whose males gather at dawn to display, and the cave known as the Cueva del Esplendor, where a waterfall falls through a hole in the roof. Birdwatchers come for the hummingbirds and tanagers that haunt the garden feeders. Rain arrives most afternoons, so plan the riding for the morning and the loitering for later.

Hot chocolate with cheese, trout from the cold streams and fried plantain cover most meals. Jardín is a small town of around eight thousand people, with several fuel stations in the area and plenty of simple guesthouses, and weekends fill up with visitors from Medellín, so book ahead if you can. Evenings are cool, and the cobbled streets, especially the steep ones, can be slippery after rain.
t.santa fe de antioquia@6.6,-75.8:
Heat is the first thing you notice here. Santa Fe de Antioquia sits low, around 500 metres above the sea in the dry canyon of the Cauca river, and after riding up out of cool Medellín and through the long tunnel under the mountains, the air thickens and the temperature leaps by ten degrees or more. The town is a grid of whitewashed colonial houses with terracotta roofs and wooden doors, a handful of stone churches, and a plaza with cafés where people sit in the shade and do very little.

It was founded in 1541, one of the earliest Spanish cities in the region, and it served as the capital of the Antioquia province until the seat of government moved to Medellín in the nineteenth century. That is why the centre is so well preserved: it simply stopped growing. Walk the quiet streets and you find carved balconies, patios full of plants, and shops selling the town's famous sweets, such as coconut and fruit pastes. During Holy Week the town fills with processions and visitors.

The real engineering marvel lies a few kilometres off. The Puente de Occidente, a suspension bridge over the Cauca, was built in the late nineteenth century by the engineer José María Villa and was for a long time among the longest bridges of its kind in Latin America. It is a lovely thing, wooden decking slung between stone towers, and you can walk across it. Vehicles are limited, so check what is allowed before trying to ride over.

The riding here is a mixture. The road down from Medellín passes through the Túnel de Occidente, one of the longest in South America, then drops to the canyon with long views of dry hills, followed by gentle curves on good tarmac. Weekend traffic can be heavy, since people from Medellín flock here, so go on a weekday if you can, and start early, because the afternoons are hot enough to test any rider in full gear.

Santa Fe de Antioquia is a town of around twelve thousand, so fuel, ice cream and cold drinks are all easy to find, and a swim in a hotel pool is the best way to end the day. Drink plenty of water, wear light layers under your protective gear, and do not leave the bike in the sun without a cover.
t.zone f@5.0,-75.9:
Zone F is one of the patches of the Coffee Cultural Landscape of Colombia, a World Heritage site spread across the steep green slopes of the Central and Western Cordilleras. This part lies in western Risaralda, around the towns of Santuario, Apía and La Celia, on hillsides so steep that you wonder how anyone stands upright to pick the beans. The answer is that people have been doing it for well over a century, by hand, on slopes where no machine could follow.

The landscape is the attraction. Coffee bushes cover the hills in neat rows, shaded by plantain and guamo trees, with stands of guadua bamboo along the streams and small farmhouses perched on the ridges. The houses are built in bahareque, a mix of bamboo and earth, with colourful balconies and tile roofs. Towns like Apía and Santuario have central plazas with churches and cafés, where farmers gather at weekends. The jeeps that carry people and sacks of coffee up and down the mountain roads, old Willys from the post-war years, are a symbol of the region.

The riding is spectacular and demanding. Roads climb and twist through the mountains with endless hairpins, steep gradients and constantly changing views. Surfaces vary from good asphalt to rough, broken concrete and dirt tracks, and landslides are common after heavy rain, which can fall at any time of year. Traffic is light but unpredictable, with jeeps, buses, trucks and animals sharing the road. A bike with good suspension and brakes will make life easier. The driest months tend to be December to February and July to August.

To the west, the Tatamá National Park protects a wild area of cloud forest and páramo, rich in birds, orchids and frogs. Colombia has more bird species than any other country, and in this region you might see toucans, tanagers and hummingbirds. The coffee harvest happens twice a year, with the main harvest in the last months of the year, when the farms are busiest.

Santuario, about five kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel, food and accommodation. Apía and La Celia also have basic services. Stop at a local café for a tinto, a small black coffee, or visit a farm to learn about the process from bush to cup, often ending with a tasting.
t.zone a@5.5,-75.7:
Colombian coffee does not grow on big estates. It grows on steep green slopes in small farms, where families pick the red cherries by hand and dry them on patios by the house, and the cultural landscape that has grown from this way of life, in the central Andes, was listed by UNESCO in 2011. The region is known as the Eje Cafetero, the coffee axis, and the Zone A on our list is one of the main areas of the property, a mix of hills, valleys and villages of small farms and old towns.

Supía and Riosucio, the nearest towns, are in the department of Caldas, and they have a particular character. Riosucio is famous for its carnival, held every two years in January, in which people dress as devils and dance through the streets in a mix of indigenous, African and Catholic traditions. The town is split between two old communities, and the people of the two sides have long had a friendly rivalry that is part of the festival. The buildings of the region, with their wooden balconies, bamboo walls plastered with mud, painted in strong colours, are typical of the area's architecture.

For a rider, the coffee region is a pleasure. Roads wind through green hills, past coffee bushes, banana plants and bamboo groves, with views over the valleys and mountains. They are often narrow and steep, with tight bends, sudden crests and old Willys jeeps loaded with sacks. Landslides after heavy rain are common, so check conditions. The rains come from March to May and from October to November, and the driest months, December to February and July to August, are the best for riding. Early starts give the best light.

Supía is about four kilometres away and has fuel, shops and small restaurants, and Riosucio, up in the hills, has more. A cup of coffee, strong and sweet, is offered everywhere, and many farms welcome visitors for a tour, showing the process from picking to roasting. Try a bandeja paisa, the hearty regional dish of beans, rice, pork, egg and plantain, and drink plenty of water, because the altitude, at around 1,800 metres in places, can sap your energy.
t.zone c@5.3,-75.5:
Zone C of the Coffee Cultural Landscape lies north of Armenia, in the steeper, higher country of Caldas, near Filadelfia and Aranzazu. This is the same UNESCO landscape, but it feels different from the Quindío end: the slopes are bigger, the farms more scattered, and the volcano Nevado del Ruiz, which looms to the east, often stands out against the sky on a clear morning. The eruption of that volcano in 1985 caused one of Colombia's worst disasters, and its presence remains part of local life.

The towns here are small and traditional, with a main square, a church and a few cafés. Filadelfia, with just over five thousand people, is a quiet coffee town, and Aranzazu is slightly larger. Neira, farther on, is a bit bigger still. Fuel is available in these towns, though Manizales, the regional capital, has far more choice. Farms along the roads put out coffee beans to dry on patios, and the smell of roasting and drying beans drifts through the villages.

The riding is intense. Roads follow ridges and twist down into river valleys, with hairpins, blind corners and sheer drops, and the surface can be rough after rain. Heavy trucks carry coffee, bananas and building materials, and the driving style is assertive. Take it slowly, sound your horn on blind bends and stay alert for landslides, which are common during the wet seasons, from April to May and October to November.

Altitude moderates the heat, so mornings are cool and the air is fresh. Bring a light jacket and rain gear. Culturally, this is paisa country, with a love of music, hospitality and strong coffee, and visitors are usually welcomed with a smile. Try a freshly brewed cup at a roadside farm, with a piece of panela, the hard brown sugar of the region, and watch the clouds roll over the hills as the afternoon turns grey.
t.segment masho piticocha@-12.1,-76.0:
High above Lima, where the desert coast gives way to the bare, windswept grasslands of the Andean puna, an old stone path crosses the mountains of Huarochirí. This is a segment of the Qhapaq Ñan, the great Inca road network that UNESCO listed in 2014, and it is one of the many trails that linked the Pacific coast with the central highlands. The region has a particular literary fame: a Quechua manuscript from around 1600, known as the Huarochirí Manuscript, records the myths and rituals of the local communities, with stories of mountain gods, floods and the great shrine of Pachacamac on the coast. It is among the few surviving texts that tell the pre-Hispanic stories in their own words.

The landscape here is raw and enormous. At four thousand metres and above, the vegetation is mostly ichu grass and cushion plants, with small glacial lakes, bog and rock. Alpacas and llamas graze beside the road, and the sky can be a deep, thin blue one moment and a wall of cloud the next. The air is cold, the wind is constant, and altitude can cause headaches and breathlessness, especially if you come straight from sea level in Lima.

No settlement of any size sits close by, which says something about the isolation. The main route into this country is the Carretera Central, which climbs from Lima along the Rímac valley, through Chosica and San Mateo, to the Ticlio pass at around 4,800 metres, one of the highest roads in the world. It is a serious road, with heavy lorries, fog, rockfalls and sudden changes of weather, and it needs patience and warm clothing. The best months are from May to October, when the days are dry and clear, though nights are freezing.

Fill the tank in Chosica or San Mateo before climbing, as there is nothing reliable higher up, and carry water, food and extra layers. Sit down at the first opportunity for a cup of coca tea or a hot soup in a roadside cafe; the pause helps your body adjust, and the cooks in these places are used to cold, tired travellers.
t.segment sisicaya santa rosa de chontay@-:
East of Lima, the Rímac valley cuts up into the Andes between brown, bare mountains, and the land here is a dry, stony slope broken by green patches of irrigated orchards and fields wherever there is water. The segment from Sisicaya to Santa Rosa de Chontay belongs to the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road network of some thirty thousand kilometres, which UNESCO listed in 2014. In this part of the world the roads connected the coastal valleys with the highlands, and a short walk along the surviving stonework gives a sense of the mountains the Incas had to cross.

The setting is typical of the Peruvian coastal foothills. There is almost no rain, the hills are pale and dusty, the sky is often hazy with the sea fog known as garúa lying over Lima, and above it the sun is hot and bright. Cacti, thorny shrubs and the occasional molle tree, with its drooping pink berries, are the main plants. Where a stream reaches the valley floor, farmers grow fruit, including chirimoya, for which this region is known, and avocado.

The nearest real towns are Chosica, a busy gateway of nearly ninety thousand people on the edge of the mountains, and the smaller places of Ricardo Palma and Nicolás de Piérola. Chosica has fuel, restaurants and markets and is a favourite weekend destination for people from Lima, because it sits above the fog and gets more sun. The Carretera Central is the key road, and it is among the most important and busiest in the country, with trucks, buses and a lot of dust. Riding it needs caution: overtaking is risky, tunnels are narrow, and the weather changes quickly as you climb.

For the best conditions, choose the dry months between May and October, clear by day and cool at night. In summer, from December to March, rain in the highlands can cause landslides and flooded washes, even when the coast is dry. Ride early in the day before the traffic builds, and stop in the villages for a plate of grilled chicken or a bowl of soup. As always in Peru, keep your wits about you with the minibuses.
t.quinta and molino de presa@-12.0,-77.0:
Lima begins in a desert, and an old country house in the Rimac district is as good a place as any to start understanding it. The Quinta and mill of Presa, a colonial estate of the eighteenth century, stands in the oldest part of the city, close to the river that gave the capital its name. The Rimac, a thin stream when it reaches the sea, brings snowmelt from the high Andes, and the whole city depends on it. Lima was founded by Francisco Pizarro in 1535 on the banks of this river, and for three centuries it was the capital of Spanish South America, so colonial houses, courtyards and balconies fill the old quarter.

The ride that begins here follows a very different, much older road. The Qhapaq Nan, the Inca road system, was a network of tens of thousands of kilometres of paved paths, stairways and rope bridges, linking the Andes from Colombia to Chile and Argentina. Relay runners called chasquis carried messages along it, and llama trains carried goods. Sections of the road were listed as a World Heritage property in 2014, and the ride visits a stretch near San Juan de Tantaranche and Huaro, in the Andean foothills inland from Lima.

Leaving the city is the first test. Lima is vast, with traffic that is dense, loud and inventive, with buses stopping anywhere, drivers who treat lane markings as suggestions, and a constant honking. The best times to start are early in the morning or on a Sunday. Once you are out on the Carretera Central, the main road up the Rimac valley, the air clears and the road climbs between bare brown mountains, with terraces and cactus on the slopes. Landslides, called huaicos, can block the road in the summer rains between January and March, and trucks and buses crowd the bends.

In winter, from June to September, a grey mist called garua covers Lima and the coast, while the Andes above are bright and dry. Altitude is a real factor on this ride, so take it slowly and drink water. Fuel stations are abundant in Lima and the larger towns on the road, but become scarce higher up, so fill up before you leave. Peruvian food is a highlight: ceviche, grilled chicken and the fruit juices from the markets, and the tiny cafes of the mountain villages serve soups and fried trout.
t.segment molle huarangal@-12.1,-76.8:
If a place could be known by its tree, Huarangal would be known by the huarango. This slow-growing, deep-rooted tree of the Peruvian coast, a kind of mesquite, once covered the dry valleys and fed the ancient people with its sweet pods, and the old Inca road passed through it. Much of the forest has been cut for charcoal and farmland, but a few trees survive, and the name of the place keeps the memory. The segment between Molle and Huarangal is a stretch of the Qhapaq Nan, the Inca road network that was listed as a World Heritage site in 2014, in the dry foothills of the Andes east of Lima, where the Rimac valley opens out and the desert meets the mountains.

The setting is stark. The hills are bare, brown and rocky, with a few green pockets where irrigation brings fields of fruit and maize, and tall cacti stand on the slopes. The air is dry, the sky clear, and the sun strong, and it is a very different place from the foggy coast. Chosica, the town nearby, is known in Lima as the sunny escape, and weekenders drive up from the grey city to find blue sky. The molle, a pepper tree with feathery leaves and pink berries, grows along the roads and gives its name to the segment.

Reaching it means riding the Carretera Central, the busy highway from Lima into the Andes, past Chosica and up the valley. Expect heavy traffic, big trucks, buses stopping on the bends and the occasional rock on the road, especially in the rainy season, between January and March, when flash floods and mud flows can cut the road. Chosica itself has suffered from such flows, and the steep dry valleys can turn in minutes. The best time for the ride is the dry season, from May to November, when the days are clear and warm, with cold nights in the high villages.

Chosica is a town of about eighty-eight thousand people, fifteen kilometres from the segment, and has fuel stations, shops, restaurants and basic hotels. Beyond it, services become sparse, so fill the tank before you start up the valley. The market stalls sell tangerines, avocados and chirimoya, the creamy custard apple that grows in the area, and in the small restaurants, trout, roast guinea pig and thick soups are on the menu. Take sun protection, water and some cash, and walk the old road with a respect for those who built it.
t.ancient reduction of santiago apostle of:
The Spanish had a word for what they did to the Andean countryside in the 1570s: reduccion. Under the viceroy Francisco de Toledo, scattered hamlets were gathered into planned towns around a plaza and a church, so that the people could be counted, taxed, taught the catechism and put to work, and a settlement named for Santiago, the apostle the conquistadors invoked in battle, was one of hundreds of such foundations. The old grid of Lima, a couple of kilometres from these coordinates, was laid out in 1535 by Francisco Pizarro on the same principle, and the whole colonial order was built on the notion that a people in straight lines is a people under control.

What the reducciones could not erase was memory. Not long after, around 1608, a priest named Francisco de Avila had a collection of local religious traditions written down in Quechua in the province of Huarochiri, east of Lima, and the Huarochiri Manuscript survives as the best account of Andean belief from before the conquest, with its mountain gods, its stories of a flood and its tale of the god Pariacaca. The Inca road that this ride follows, the Qhapaq Nan, ran through these same valleys, and the old stone paths still climb out of the Rimac valley above the sprawl of the capital.

Lima does not make it easy to leave. The city of nearly eight million people spreads along the desert coast, hemmed between the Pacific and the foothills, and the traffic is a sport of its own: buses that stop wherever a passenger waves, vans with a conductor leaning out of the door shouting destinations, and drivers who read the horn as a language. Start on a Sunday morning or before dawn if you can, and use the main avenues and the expressway along the cliffs, the Costa Verde, rather than the grid of the old centre, where one-way streets and market stalls turn every junction into a negotiation.

Everything a rider needs is within reach here: fuel stations on every corner, workshops that can fix almost anything, cheap lunch menus with soup, rice and a main dish. In winter, from about June to October, a low grey cloud called the garua smothers the coast, the damp gets into everything, and the sun is a rumour, while the mountains above are often bright and dry. Fill up and eat before heading up the Rimac valley, because services thin out quickly past the last suburbs. Carry some small notes for tolls and for the people who will offer to watch your bike. The ride to Molle and Huarangal follows the old way inland, and the climb into clean air is a pleasure after the city.
t.al quwayr@34.2,43.8:
Samarra was once the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate, the empire that ruled the Islamic world from Baghdad. In the ninth century the caliph al-Mu'tasim moved his court and army about a hundred kilometres up the Tigris to a new site, and for around half a century the city grew into an enormous sprawl of palaces, mosques, barracks and gardens stretching along the river for tens of kilometres. When the capital returned to Baghdad in the 890s, Samarra was abandoned, which is why so much of its plan survives as ruins and mounds rather than being built over by later cities.

The northern zone, called al-Mutawakkiliyya after the caliph al-Mutawakkil, who built a new quarter here, contains some of the grandest remains. The Great Mosque, with its spiral minaret, the Malwiya, rises about fifty metres above the plain and was among the largest mosques in the world at the time, and the surrounding enclosure walls still mark out an immense courtyard. Al-Quwayr, a palace site in the same area, is part of this great field of ruins and gives a sense of how the caliphs built on a scale that matched their ambitions. I do not know the particulars of the individual structures here, so I would not pretend to guide you around them, but the setting is clear enough: a flat, dry plain of baked earth, with the river to the west and the faint outlines of vanished courtyards.

Practical matters need care here. Samarra is a large city of around a hundred and fifty thousand and has fuel, shops and food, but Iraq's security situation, the condition of the roads and the rules for foreign visitors can change quickly, and travel by motorbike is unusual. Anyone thinking of visiting should check current government advice and local conditions, and should not assume access to archaeological sites.

The landscape is stark and beautiful in its own way. The Tigris cuts a wide, silt-brown line through a country of dust, date palms, and low hills, and the summers are fierce, with temperatures that can pass forty-five degrees. Spring is the kinder season, when the plain turns briefly green, and the air is clear.

The spiral minaret has a ramp winding up the outside, a shape so unusual that it has become the symbol of the city.
t.kone@-21.1,164.9:
Koné is where New Caledonia stops looking like a holiday brochure and starts looking like a working island. The town sits on the west coast of the Grande Terre, about halfway up, in a dry plain of savanna and cattle ranches, and it has been the administrative centre of the Northern Province since the province was created in the 1980s. The pin lies at the edge of the town, with the Pacific a few kilometres west and the central mountain range, which runs the length of the island like a spine, rising to the east.

The landscape is surprising. The west coast is drier than the east, with open grassland dotted with niaouli trees, whose pale papery bark peels in layers, and herds of cattle that belong to the descendants of European stockmen, the Caldoches, who settled here in the nineteenth century. Nearby, the huge Koniambo massif is the site of a nickel smelter, a reminder that the island's wealth comes from the red earth. Along the coast, mangrove swamps line the lagoon, and near Voh, a clearing in the mangroves forms a perfect heart shape that became famous in an aerial photograph.

The main road, the RT1, runs the length of the west coast, and it is a good ride. The surface is generally smooth, the bends are gentle, and the views alternate between the lagoon and the mountains. In the dry season, from about May to November, the weather is warm and bright, and the roads are quiet. From January to March, cyclones can bring heavy rain and flooding, and roads may be cut at river crossings. Drive on the right, watch for cattle on the road, and beware of the midday heat.

Fuel is available in Koné, a town of about four and a half thousand, and in Pouembout and Voh nearby. Small restaurants serve fresh fish, venison and the island's blend of French and Pacific cooking, and the local bakeries open early, with excellent baguettes. Cash in Pacific francs is useful, as cards are not accepted everywhere. The Kanak culture of the island is strong here, so ask before visiting tribal land and treat the customs of the tribes with respect.
t.huacachina@-14.1,-75.8:
Huacachina is the kind of place that looks like a joke the Peruvian desert is playing on you. A small lagoon, ringed with palms and old-fashioned lamp posts, sits in a bowl of enormous sand dunes five kilometres from the city of Ica. Local legend says it formed when a princess, bathing, saw a hunter, dropped her mirror and fled; the mirror became the lake, and her robe the dunes. The truth is rather drier, a natural spring that has been dwindling for decades as water is pumped out for farms nearby.

Whatever the origin, the oasis is a Peruvian weekend favourite. Dune buggies roar over the crests, sandboarders slide down, and the little tourist village around the water has cafes, hostels and pisco bars. It is touristy and a little scruffy, but the dunes are the real thing: ridge after ridge of pale gold, rising over a hundred metres, and the light at sunset turns them copper and rose. A rider who has been down the Pan-American Highway all day will find the place a reasonable excuse to stop, and a sunset walk to the top of a dune is the sort of effort that justifies a cold beer.

Ica itself is a city of more than two hundred thousand people, and has everything: fuel at every junction, banks, markets, restaurants. It sits in a dry valley that is, strangely, wine country, and Ica is the home of Peruvian pisco, the grape brandy at the base of a pisco sour. Vineyards and small bodegas are scattered through the valley, and some welcome visitors for a tasting, though a motorcyclist should taste with a straw hat rather than a glass.

The ride in is easy. The Pan-American Highway runs south from Lima across the coastal desert with the Pacific to the west and the Andes foothills to the east, a long dry corridor of sand, scrub and occasional green river valleys. Wind is the thing to respect, particularly in the afternoon, when gusts blow sand across the tarmac and push a loaded bike around. Trucks are heavy on the main road, so be careful overtaking.

Sand creeps into everything here, so cover the bike's air intake and zip your luggage. In the cooler months the nights are chilly, and the coast is often shrouded in the grey garua mist, while Huacachina itself stays sunny and dry.
t.manizales@5.1,-75.5:
Manizales is a city built on a ridge, and it takes some getting used to. The streets climb and fall at gradients that make a bicycle useless and a motorcycle a sensible choice, and at about 2,150 metres the air is cool and often misty. The city is the capital of Caldas, a coffee department, and it was founded in the middle of the nineteenth century by settlers from Antioquia who cut their way into the forest to plant coffee.

Above it all stands the Nevado del Ruiz, an active volcano more than five thousand metres high, whose snow-capped summit appears on clear mornings and disappears in cloud for days. The mountain's eruption in 1985 caused a catastrophic mudflow that destroyed the town of Armero, and the memory is still strong across the region; the volcano is closely monitored, and access to the national park around it is sometimes restricted. The road up toward it climbs through high moorland, with frailejones, fuzzy-leaved plants that look like silver-green stalks, and ends at a cold, windy landscape of grey rock.

In the city itself, the cathedral is the landmark, a tall concrete-and-stone structure whose tower rises over the centre, and visitors can climb it for a view over the rooftops and across the mountains. There is a cable car that links the centre to the bus terminal and beyond, and the central square is a good place to sit with a coffee and watch the life of the city. Manizales has a university tradition and a lively evening scene, and the coffee, naturally, is excellent.

The roads in and out are mountain roads, with steep climbs, tight bends and heavy truck traffic, and the weather can change in minutes from sun to fog to rain. Take care on wet pavement and watch for slow trucks on the approach. With nearly 360,000 people in the city and Villamaría next door, fuel and services are plentiful, and it is the best place in the region to fill the tank and get supplies.

The best months are December to February and July to August, but the mountains make their own weather, so carry a rain jacket whenever you ride. Early mornings are the clearest, and the volcano is most likely to show itself then.
t.guatape@6.2,-75.2:
Guatapé is a lakeside town in the hills east of Medellín, and its fame rests on two things: the colour of its streets and a giant rock. The houses are decorated along the lower walls with painted reliefs known as zócalos, showing scenes of family life, animals, flowers and local trades, and every street is a gallery in bright blues, reds, greens and yellows. The effect is playful and the town takes it seriously, with each building competing to look better than its neighbours.

The rock is El Peñol, a huge granite monolith, a single mass of stone rising some two hundred metres above the water. A stairway of several hundred steps has been built into a crack on its side, and the climb to the top rewards you with a view over a maze of islands, peninsulas and green water. The lake itself is a reservoir, created in the 1970s when a river was dammed for hydroelectric power, flooding the valley and the old town of El Peñol, whose people were moved to a new settlement. The drowned landscape explains the jigsaw shape of the shoreline, with hills turned into islands.

The ride from Medellín takes you up out of the Aburrá valley and over the hills of the Oriente, along a good paved road with long bends, views of rolling green farmland and a constant stream of buses, trucks and weekend traffic. On Sundays and holidays the road is crowded with visitors, and patience is needed behind slow vehicles. In the early morning it is calmer and cooler, and the light on the hills is soft.

Guatapé is a town of about five thousand and has fuel and food, with plenty of restaurants serving the local plate of beans, rice, pork, egg and avocado, along with fresh trout from the lake. Boats take visitors around the reservoir, and a stroll along the waterfront is pleasant at sunset. The climate is mild, around twenty degrees in the day, with showers common in the afternoon, so a rain jacket is useful. The best time to climb the rock is the morning, before the haze rises.
t.alto de las palmas@6.2,-75.5:
Medellín lies in a narrow valley at about 1,500 metres, and the road out of it to the east climbs sharply to the Alto de Las Palmas, 2,550 metres above sea level, in a long series of curves above the city. At the top, a viewpoint looks back over the whole Aburrá Valley, with the city's towers laid out in a ribbon far below and the cloud often curling over the ridges. It is one of the classic views of the city, and on a clear evening, when the lights come on, it is hard to leave.

The road is a favourite with local riders and cyclists, who come here on weekends in large numbers. The gradient is steady, the bends are open and well surfaced, and trucks grind up in low gear, so overtaking calls for judgement. Cloud and drizzle are common near the top, reducing visibility, and the temperature falls enough to make a jacket welcome. The road continues downhill on the other side toward Rionegro and the plateau that holds the international airport, with a different landscape of gentle hills, flower farms and cooler air.

The surrounding area is part of the Colombian Andes, where the Central Cordillera is covered in forest and farmland. Pines and eucalyptus planted decades ago line sections of the road, and there are still patches of native cloud forest on steeper slopes. Birdlife is rich, and mornings bring a loud chorus. Antioquia's farming culture is strong, and roadside stalls and restaurants serve local food, including the hearty bandeja paisa, a platter of beans, rice, pork and plantain that can defeat any appetite.

As a practical matter, Medellín and its neighbouring towns, such as Envigado and Sabaneta, have plenty of fuel, workshops and food. On the climb itself there are service stations and restaurants, but check your tank before you start. Weekend traffic can be heavy, and security advice for Colombian roads is worth reading, particularly regarding where to park and what to leave on the bike. Stay on well-travelled routes and ride in daylight.

Mornings are best, when the air is clear and the city is quiet. Later in the day, the mist often settles and the road feels more like the high Andes than a suburban escape.
t.el retiro@6.1,-75.5:
El Retiro is the sort of Antioquian mountain town where people from Medellín come to eat lunch and then pretend to consider moving. It lies on the plateau east of the city, in cool, green country at over two thousand metres, with a tidy square, a church, a handful of craft shops and a mood of unhurried prosperity. The surrounding hills are a patchwork of farms, flower nurseries and weekend homes, and the climate is a relief after the heat of the valley, though it can be damp and misty.

The town has a reputation for woodwork. Carpenters here make furniture and decorative pieces, and you will find workshops and shops selling tables, chairs and carved details along the roads into town. It also has a strong tradition of local cooking, with restaurants serving trout, grilled meat and thick soups. On weekends, the main square fills with families and riders, and the pace of life gently speeds up.

The ride from Medellín over Las Palmas and down toward Retiro is a satisfying one. The road drops from the high ridge into the plateau in a series of bends, passing through farmland and pine woods, with views of green hills fading into mist. After the climb, the surface is generally good, and the traffic is mostly local cars and farm vehicles. From Retiro, roads lead to La Ceja, a larger town with more shops, and toward Rionegro, with more roads into the hills for those who want to keep exploring. Some side roads are narrower and rougher, and landslides can occur after heavy rain.

El Retiro has about eight thousand people, enough to have fuel, a bank and supermarkets, so it is a practical place to rest and refuel. If you need more services, La Ceja, a few kilometres away, is bigger. The local bakeries sell fresh bread and sweet treats, and a hot chocolate with cheese, a Colombian habit that sounds odd until you try it, is a common order on cool mornings.

The rain here is regular, and sudden showers are normal, so a waterproof layer is more than a precaution. Sunshine comes in bright spells, making the hills look washed and the colours deep.
t.bala@45.0,-79.6:
Bala has two claims to fame, and both are good ones. In October it holds the Cranberry Festival, built around the bogs that surround the village, where the berries are harvested by flooding the beds so they float to the surface in a red carpet. And in the middle of the twentieth century it was one of the places in Ontario where you went to dance: the Kee to Bala, a lakeside hall, hosted big bands and then rock acts for generations, and a lot of grandparents in southern Ontario met each other there.

The village sits where Lake Muskoka drains into the Moon River over a set of falls, in the granite country of the Canadian Shield. The rock is pink and grey, scrubbed by ice, and the lakes are dark, clear and cold. Lucy Maud Montgomery, who wrote Anne of Green Gables, visited Bala in the 1920s and drew on the district for her novel The Blue Castle, and there is a small museum in the village that makes much of it. The falls in the centre of town are a pleasant surprise for a place that seems built mostly for boats and cottages.

The roads that bring you here, mostly the Muskoka district roads that thread between the lakes, are twisting, rolling and quite narrow. The bedrock forces the engineers to build around outcrops, which means a constant series of short rises and bends, with pine and birch pressing in on both sides. They are best on a weekday, because the cottage traffic arrives on Friday evening and leaves on Sunday afternoon, and then the lakes road becomes a slow line of trailers carrying boats. Watch for deer at dusk and for gravel washed onto the tarmac in spring.

Bala is small enough that fuel is hit and miss in the off season, so plan to top up in Gravenhurst or Bracebridge, each about twenty-odd kilometres away, both of them real towns with all services. The village itself is good for ice cream, a sit-down lunch and a walk at the falls. Autumn colour comes in the first half of October, usually just in time for the festival, and the crowds follow it.
t.port carling@45.1,-79.6:
Port Carling exists because of a lock. In 1871 a short canal with a lock was cut through the narrows between Lake Rosseau and Lake Muskoka, joining the two lakes and opening up the whole chain for steamers that carried settlers, supplies and, later, summer visitors. A century and a half later the lock is still working, and from a bench beside it you can watch pleasure boats, some of them very expensive and very polished, rise and fall in the chamber while a small crowd stands by with ice cream.

The village has been the centre of Muskoka boat building for as long as anyone remembers. The wooden launches and runabouts that were built here are collector's pieces now, and a good deal of the local economy still depends on cottage owners with a taste for varnish. The Muskoka Lakes Museum, near the lock, tells some of the story, and the old steamship RMS Segwun, launched in the 1880s and said to be the oldest operating steamship in North America, still sails from Gravenhurst, a reminder of what travel here looked like before the roads.

By motorcycle, Port Carling is a calm, rolling landscape of low granite hills, lakes and white pines. The roads leading in and out follow the water, with plenty of blind curves, short climbs and sudden views across a lake or a bay, and the tarmac is mostly sound, with more potholes in spring. The pace is slow by necessity, since the speed limits are low and the shoulders are narrow; the countryside rewards a relaxed ride rather than an urgent one. On summer weekends the bridge and the main street fill with cars, so a morning visit gives you a quieter lock and an easier parking spot.

For fuel, Bracebridge, about twenty-three kilometres away, is the nearest bigger place, with every kind of station, and Gravenhurst is a little further. The village has a few places for coffee, a bakery and a couple of pubs, but the options shrink after Labour Day. If you want somewhere to sit by the water, the park near the lock is the obvious place, and the grass is cooler than the road. In October, when the maples and birches turn, the whole district glows, and the cottages are mostly shut.
t.rosseau@45.3,-79.6:
Rosseau is the quiet one of the three Muskoka stops. It lies at the northern end of Lake Rosseau, in a country of bare granite, black water and thin pine, and it is smaller, calmer and a good deal less manicured than Port Carling. In the nineteenth century this was a frontier: a colonisation road was pushed through the bush from Parry Sound on Georgian Bay, and the lake steamers met it here, so that settlers and goods could carry on by water into the heart of Muskoka. The land turned out to be far poorer for farming than the government had hoped, with soil that barely covered the rock, and a lot of the early farms failed, which is why the region turned to logging and then to tourism.

That history explains the landscape. Many of the roads follow the old routes, and they have a purposeful, slightly crooked feel, with rock cuts, short steep pitches, one-lane bridges and frost-heave bumps. The rock cuts are a pleasure on a bike: pink and grey granite, scraped by glaciers, with birch roots clinging to the top. Traffic is lighter than around Bracebridge and Port Carling, though the weekend cottage flow still reaches here, and there are logging trucks and the occasional tractor. Deer are plentiful at dusk, and in autumn the sumac and red maple are brilliant against the dark conifers.

The village has an old-fashioned centre with a small store, a few places to eat and a waterfront that looks across the bay. It feels like a place that has been a summer resort for more than a century, with old wooden lodges and cottages along the shore, but it has not been polished into a showpiece. A mooch along the water, a coffee and a slow ride out again is a good use of an hour.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Rosseau itself is small, so do not rely on it; Parry Sound, about thirty kilometres to the west on Georgian Bay, is the nearest town of any size, and Huntsville is a similar distance to the north-east. Fill up at one of them before you come in. The lake is lovely in the evening, when the wind drops and the water goes flat, and the mosquitoes come out, so keep a jacket handy.
t.the colonial transisthmian route of pana:
The Camino Real, the royal road that Spain built across the Isthmus of Panama in the sixteenth century, is the reason this country matters in world history. Gold and silver from Peru were carried by ship to Panama City, loaded on mules and carried over the continental divide to the Caribbean coast, then shipped to Spain. The route had two arms: a paved mule road, the Camino Real, to Portobelo, and a mixed river-and-trail route, the Camino de Cruces, which used the Chagres River for part of the way. Together with the forts that guarded them, the Caribbean forts at Portobelo and San Lorenzo are on the UNESCO list, listed in 1980.

For a rider, the Caribbean end of the story starts around Colon, a rough and rundown city at the mouth of the canal. The road from Panama City, crossing the isthmus in roughly an hour and a half, passes the Gatun Locks, where a steel swing bridge takes you across the canal chamber while ships rise and fall. Beyond it, narrow roads lead through jungle toward the Chagres River and the old fort at San Lorenzo, past howler monkeys, toucans and troops of white-faced capuchins. The tarmac is patchy, with potholes, and heavy rain from May to December can leave it slick.

The isthmus is narrow, and that is the whole point. Standing on a hillside you can nearly imagine how the Spaniards, pirates and later gold-rush travellers all squeezed through this one gap between the oceans. The English privateer Henry Morgan came this way in 1671, capturing the fort at San Lorenzo and marching across to burn Panama City. The old Spanish city is now a ruin, and a newer capital stands further along the bay.

Practical matters need care. Colon has fuel and a handful of restaurants, but it has a reputation for petty crime, so keep valuables out of sight and avoid walking at night. The jungle stretches have few stations, so fill the tank before leaving the main road. The dry season, from January to April, makes for the easiest riding. The humid heat is strong all year, and a rain jacket is always useful.
t.castle of san lorenzo@9.3,-80.0:
The Castle of San Lorenzo stands on a cliff at the mouth of the Chagres River, on the Caribbean coast of Panama, and it was built to stop pirates. Gold and silver came across the isthmus on the Camino Real and the river, and this stone fort guarded the river mouth from the sea. Construction began in the late sixteenth century, and the fort, with its ditch, ramparts and cannon, was a serious piece of military engineering. It did not hold forever. In 1671 Henry Morgan and a force of buccaneers took it after a fierce fight in which the Spanish defenders resisted until their thatched roofs caught fire. Morgan went on to sack Panama City.

The place is lovely and wild. From the top of the cliff you look out over the sea on one side and the brown, slow-moving Chagres on the other, with dense jungle spreading in every direction. Waves crash on the rocks below, and the old walls are green with moss and creepers. A fine, damp smell hangs over everything. The Chagres is the river that feeds Gatun Lake, and thus the Panama Canal, so the water that floats the ships begins here.

The road to the fort is half the pleasure. From Colon you cross the canal at the Gatun Locks, then follow a narrow road through the former Canal Zone, past the old American base of Fort Sherman, now partly returned to the jungle. The road passes under dense canopy, with barracks and old buildings half hidden in the trees. Bends are tight and the surface is rough, with roots and potholes. A few vendors sell cold drinks and fruit near the fort. In the wet season, between May and December, the road is muddy and visibility is poor, and in the dry months it is dustier but easier.

Birdwatchers will find plenty to look at, with trogons, motmots and tanagers around the entrance. Monkeys call from the trees, and the occasional crocodile lies on the river bank. Be careful of the cliffs, since there are few railings. Colon, eleven kilometres away, has fuel and basic food, though conditions there are rough. Bring water, insect repellent and a rain jacket, and give yourself a morning here rather than an hour.
t.panama city@9.0,-79.5:
Panama City is the only capital in the world with a rainforest inside its limits, and a canal at its door. The city curves round a bay on the Pacific side, with a skyline of glass towers that looks more like Miami than anything in Central America, and behind it the old quarter, Casco Viejo, is a peninsula of balconied houses, plazas and church towers rebuilt after the pirate Henry Morgan sacked the first settlement in 1671. The ruins of that first city, Panamá Viejo, still stand a few kilometres east, with a bell tower you can climb.

The Canal is what made the place. The Americans completed it in 1914, after the French failed, and it still lifts ships over the isthmus in giant locks. At Miraflores you can stand beside the lock and watch a vessel taller than a building slide past at walking pace. Across the Bridge of the Americas, the road leads west to the old Spanish fortress at San Lorenzo, which sits on a headland at the mouth of the Chagres river, to guard the route along which Spanish gold once moved from the Pacific to the Caribbean. The rides here lead into that jungle and history.

Riding in the city needs care. Traffic is dense and aggressive, lanes are suggestions, and the rain, when it comes in the wet season from May to December, falls in great afternoon downpours that turn the roads slick and the drains into rivers. The dry season from January to April is much easier, with blue skies and a steady breeze. Once you get out through the Canal area, the roads on the Gatun side run through thick green forest with tall trees, hanging vines and the sound of birds, and you might see toucans, monkeys or a sloth in the roadside trees.

Fuel is easy in the city, with modern stations everywhere. Pack a rain jacket whatever the forecast, as the sky can turn quickly. Ceviche and fried fish at the fish market by the bay is a real local lunch, and the coffee in Casco Viejo is as good as any in the region.
t.al huwaysilat upper@34.3,43.8:
Samarra has one of the strangest histories of any city on earth. In 836 the Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tasim, annoyed by clashes between his Turkish soldiers and the people of Baghdad, moved the entire court some 125 kilometres up the Tigris and built a new capital on the east bank. For about fifty-six years, until 892, it was the seat of the caliphate, a sprawling city of palaces, mosques, racecourses and barracks, and then it was abandoned, left to the desert. The result is an archaeological site of immense size, stretching for over thirty kilometres along the river, and it was listed by UNESCO in 2007.

The label al-Huwaysilat belongs to that ruined landscape, and I cannot honestly name a specific building at this pin. What you can see is the same terrain as everywhere around Samarra: a flat, pale plain by the Tigris, scattered with mounds of mud-brick, low walls and the outlines of courtyards that were once part of palaces. The soil is silty and almost white in the heat, with irrigated date palms and cultivation near the river and a hard, empty steppe a short way back.

Riding here means flat, straight roads, with long views and dust. Highway 1 runs along the Tigris between Baghdad, Samarra and Tikrit, and it is a busy road with trucks and local traffic, so overtaking needs care. Summers are brutal, with temperatures above forty-five degrees, and the best time to visit is from October to April, when the days are mild. Dust storms can reduce visibility sharply in spring. The security situation in this part of Iraq has varied in recent years, so check current travel advice and local conditions before you plan any trip.

Samarra is a city of about 160,000 people, about fourteen kilometres from here, and has fuel stations, shops and simple restaurants. Tikrit, farther north, is another option, though it is nearly forty kilometres away. Carry water and sun protection. The Askari shrine, with its golden dome, is the city's great pilgrimage site, and the spiral minaret of the Great Mosque, the Malwiya, is the best-known monument. Ask locally about access and etiquette before visiting either.
t.al istablat@34.1,43.9:
Al-Istablat is one of the outlying sites of the Abbasid capital at Samarra, and its name, which echoes the Arabic for stables, hints at the scale of a court that kept thousands of horses and cavalrymen. The pin falls on the plain south of the main city, about thirteen kilometres from Samarra and a shorter distance from Balad, on the road toward Baghdad. I cannot describe the particular remains at this exact point with confidence, but the neighbourhood is part of the archaeological zone and shares its character.

The ground here is flat and fertile near the Tigris, with fields of wheat, barley and vegetables fed by irrigation canals, some of them descended from Abbasid works, and the river itself is wide and brown, with reeds and willows along the bank. A little way back from the water the land becomes dry steppe, with scrubby bushes and patches of salt. In winter, flocks of ducks and waders feed on the wetlands, and storks pass through on migration. Further out, the desert begins in earnest, and distances look much shorter than they are.

For a rider, this belongs to the long, flat road between Baghdad and Samarra, about 125 kilometres in all, along Highway 1, through Balad and past farms, roadside stalls and army checkpoints. The surface is generally good but heavily used by lorries, and local drivers overtake in the face of oncoming traffic, so keep your distance and stay alert. Midsummer heat is intense, and the road shimmers, so start early and carry plenty of water. Dust storms appear in spring and early summer, and rain in winter can turn dirt tracks to mud.

Samarra is the nearest large town, with services including fuel, food and mechanics, and Balad, about twenty kilometres away, also has facilities. Beyond them the choices thin, so fill up early. The tea in a roadside stall is strong, served in small glasses with plenty of sugar, and bread and kebabs are the usual meal. Security conditions in Iraq can change quickly, so check official travel advice and talk to local people about the safest routes before you set out.
t.al huwaysilat lower@34.3,43.8:
The lower of the two sites called al-Huwaysilat sits on the same bank of the Tigris as the upper one, and in practice they run into each other, which is what happens when a caliph's city stretches for thirty kilometres. I cannot say what stood at this exact spot, but the story of the city around it is a good one. Samarra's name was said to come from a phrase meaning that he who sees it is delighted, though the Arabs also joked that it was a place where a man who saw it was grieved, and the court's brief life there suggests that both were true.

What the Abbasids understood best was water. The river was the lifeblood of the capital, and they dug long canals to bring it to gardens, palaces and fields. The land is flat, silty and pale, and in the green belt beside the river grow date palms, pomegranates and vegetables, while the dry plain beyond stretches out to a sky that fills most of the view. At sunrise, the light on the ruined walls is warm and soft, and the shadows are long.

Practicalities matter more than usual here. Highway 1 follows the river, and the road is a fast one, with drivers who treat the white line as a suggestion. Spring is pleasant, with green fields and wildflowers, but summer is fierce, with temperatures that can rise above 48 degrees, so it is wise to ride early and rest in the shade at midday. Winter nights can be cold. Before planning a visit, read the latest travel advice, because the security situation in Salah ad-Din province has varied.

Samarra, fifteen kilometres from the pin, has fuel and food, and Tikrit is the next larger town to the north, at around thirty-seven kilometres. Carry spare water, a basic toolkit and a charged phone, as help may be some distance away. Locals are usually friendly and curious, and a rider who stops to look at the ruins is likely to be offered tea. Ask permission before photographing people or military installations, and remember that the golden-domed shrine in the city is a living place of worship.
t.qubbat al sulaibiyya@34.2,43.8:
Qubbat al-Sulaibiyya is a small building with a large claim. It is a domed mausoleum from the 860s at Samarra, and it is generally considered to be the earliest surviving tomb of an Abbasid caliph, built for al-Muntasir, who ruled for only six months in 861 and 862, after the murder of his father al-Mutawakkil. Two later caliphs, al-Mu'tazz and al-Muhtadi, are believed to have been buried there too, which gives it a grim sort of importance. The structure is an octagonal chamber surrounded by an octagonal corridor, set inside a square enclosure, a plan that influenced later tombs across the Islamic world.

It stands on the eastern edge of the old capital, about nine kilometres from modern Samarra, on a flat plain beside the Tigris. The building is made of baked brick, once covered in plaster, and its surrounding wall is cut with niches, and the weathered, earth-coloured structure rises very simply out of the empty ground. Around it are old fields and clumps of tamarisk. Nothing else is nearby, and the silence of the place can be striking, with only the wind in the dry grass.

The nearest main road is Highway 1, the busy artery between Baghdad and the north, and you reach the site by smaller tracks that can be rough or sandy. A bike with decent ground clearance is better than a low tourer, and after rain the clay turns slick and sticky. The heat in summer can be extreme and the plain is shadeless, so plan your visit for early morning or late afternoon. Winter and early spring are the best seasons. Security conditions in the area have changed over the years, so look for up-to-date guidance and local advice before going.

Samarra, nine kilometres away, has fuel stations, basic restaurants and shops, while Balad, to the south, is a bigger town, though it lies about forty kilometres from the pin. Take water for the whole day and food if you have a long stay. Visit the Great Mosque with its spiral minaret, the Malwiya, which stands about fifty-two metres tall and was among the largest mosques in the world when it was built, and treat all religious sites with respect.
t.poum@-20.2,164.0:
Poum is where the road runs out of patience. It lies at the far north-western tip of Grande Terre, on a coast that faces the open lagoon and the reefs beyond, and you arrive after hours of travel through ranchland, scrub and small villages. The place is tiny, with a population in the low thousands at most, a handful of shops, a church and a scattered seaside life that moves at the speed of the tide.

The country around is the real draw. Bush savannah dotted with niaouli trees, with their pale, papery bark, gives way to mangroves along the shore and views over a lagoon that is part of the New Caledonia lagoons listed by UNESCO. Dugongs and sea turtles live in these waters, though you are unlikely to see them from the road. The land here is quiet cattle country, where stockmen on horseback are still a common sight, and people take pride in a laid-back, rural identity that is a world away from Nouméa.

The riding is a pleasure of a particular kind. The road along the west coast is mostly well-surfaced and winding without being demanding, with long gentle bends through low hills, and wide views of the lagoon. There is little traffic once you leave the south, which tempts you to go faster than the surface deserves; potholes, loose gravel at the verges and livestock on the tarmac can all surprise you. The last stretch towards Poum narrows and the settlements spread out, which is part of its appeal.

Be sensible with fuel. Poum is small and I would not count on a station being open at the hour you need it, so plan to fill up in a larger place such as Koné or Pouembout along the way before the final push north. Water, snacks and a spare layer in case of showers are cheap insurance.

Time the visit for the dry season, roughly May to October, when the air is clear and the heat is manageable. In the wet season rain can arrive suddenly and rivers rise across the road. At the end you can sit on the shore, watch the light fade over the lagoon, and feel that you have genuinely reached the far side of an island.
